::: {.why}
The variance premium is real and the strategies that harvest it have destroyed more capital than most, which makes this the clearest case in the year of a positive expected return being insufficient.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Name three distinct ways to be short volatility and say how their payoffs differ in a fast move.
- Describe what happened to short-volatility products in February 2018 in mechanical terms.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Compare the three: selling a delta-hedged straddle, selling a variance swap, and holding a short VIX futures position. Simulate a fast volatility spike and report each one's loss. They differ substantially because a variance swap's payoff is quadratic in the move while a delta-hedged option's is not, and a VIX future is a bet on the term structure rather than on realized variance at all.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Work through the February 2018 mechanics: an inverse volatility product rebalances to a constant short exposure daily, so a large volatility rise forces buying at the close into the move, which raises volatility further. Write the mechanism out and note that it is the same forced-deleveraging structure as day 13's margin spiral.
:::
:::
